justice: The physical separation of the wide roadway and side paths allocates space for both drivers and vulnerable users, reflecting basic spatial equity.
The flat and obstacle-free sidewalks provide fundamental accessibility for wheelchair users and strollers, though the vast scale may be exhausting for the elderly.
The lack of visible tactile paving in the pedestrian zones reduces fairness and independent mobility for visually impaired individuals.
safety: Planted side medians physically separate motor vehicles from cyclists and pedestrians, significantly enhancing safety for vulnerable road users.
Metal guardrails at the central median prevent dangerous mid-block crossings by pedestrians and teenagers.
Tall street lighting poles spaced regularly along the road ensure nighttime visibility and security for drivers and pedestrians.
livability: The complete absence of ground-floor commercial facades or residential buildings results in a lack of urban vitality and destinations for all social groups.
There are no visible public gathering spaces or plazas, reducing opportunities for social interaction among the elderly and teenagers.
The lack of 'eyes on the street' due to missing pedestrian activity makes the environment feel isolated and less supportive of a vibrant community life.
sustainability: Continuous planting strips with young trees provide a foundation for future urban greening and ecological benefits.
The large expanse of impermeable asphalt pavement for multiple vehicle lanes limits natural rainwater infiltration.
The absence of visible public transit infrastructure, such as bus shelters, hinders the promotion of low-carbon shared travel options.
aesthetics: The newly paved, clean road surface and orderly lane markings create a visually tidy and well-maintained streetscape.
The open sky view and distant mountains provide a pleasant natural macro-scale backdrop for drivers and pedestrians.
The landscaping in the central median with yellow flowers adds a necessary touch of color to an otherwise monotonous grey infrastructure.
comfort: The young, bare street trees currently provide no canopy shade, leading to poor thermal comfort for pedestrians and cyclists during hot weather.
The complete lack of street furniture, such as benches, heavily reduces physical comfort for elderly pedestrians who require frequent rest.
The smooth, flat paving in the separated side lanes supports physically comfortable movement for cyclists and wheelchair users.
walkability: The physical separation of the sidewalk by green buffers provides a safe walking route away from fast-moving traffic.
The lack of visible crosswalks or intersections in the immediate foreground severely limits pedestrian route connectivity and convenience.
The absence of active street frontages and shading makes the walking experience visually unappealing and tiring for pedestrians.
bikeability: The wide, physically separated side roads offer a highly safe and protected environment for cyclists of all ages.
The smooth asphalt surface in the non-motorized lanes ensures a comfortable and efficient riding experience without bumps.
The lack of distinct bicycle lane markings within the side paths may cause right-of-way confusion between cyclists and local pedestrians.
